title: Rav Hamnuna (I)

paragraphs: The teacher of Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi’s student, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.2.9): Rabbi was sitting and teaching — Rabbi Chanina said to him, “Humot.” He said to him, “Where did you read it?” He said to him, “Before Rav Hamnuna in Babylonia.” In [Kohelet Rabbah 7:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Kohelet_Rabbah.7.7.2) he is called Rav Hamnuna the scribe of Babylonia. Hyman conjectures that what they said in [Menachot 17a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.17a.10), “Rav Hamnuna said: This matter was instilled in me at Rabbi Chanina’s, and it is worth as much to me as all my learning,” concerns Rav Hamnuna, Rabbi Chanina’s teacher; see his entry. But [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Menachot.17a.10.1) explains, “he gave me a taste and taught me.” If so, Hyman infers that the passage concerns Rav Hamnuna (III) and that the Rabbi Chanina in it is the “colleague of the rabbis,” whom Hyman identifies as Rabbah’s brother.

notes.text: The printed quotation includes בי, “at the house of,” while the consulted Menachot text has Rabbi Chanina directly as the one who taught the matter. This supports Rashi’s idiomatic reading. Hyman’s identification of the two sages remains his inference.

The value idiom תקילא עלי is rendered “is worth as much to me,” rather than suggesting that the teaching is a burden. Davidson Menachot 17a English similarly calls it equivalent to all the speaker’s learning. The original note’s הן קריתה is understood as היכן קריתה, “where did you read it?”; neither that contextual reading nor the named Talmud proves Hyman’s printed letters.

Hyman’s printed entry (vol. I, p. 376) reads חברון דרבנן אחי רבה, with a final nun in חברון. The supplied digital text reads חברו. “Colleague of the rabbis” is attested in Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 1:6 and, with a different spelling, Ketubot 11:5. In Hyman’s separate entry on Rav Chananya (vol. II, pp. 500–502), he identifies him with the sage who bears that title. He attributes the claim of brotherhood to Yuchasin and Maharsha, says he found no source for it himself, and proposes a reconstruction. The Yerushalmi passages cited here attest the title. Hyman’s reconstruction links the sage bearing that title with Rabbah’s brother and with the Chanina in Menachot.
